title: POC scaling ramp and fallback plan - Phoenix Retailers
summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on capacity sizing for a 6-week pilot. Customer wants reserved GPU baseline plus controlled burst for peak shopping windows, with clear success metrics (latency 95th < 350ms, cost per 1k tokens target, no PII leakage). Agreed next steps: Redwood to send SOW and benchmark template; Phoenix to share sample traffic and compliance checklist; schedule infra test week of 11/9.
next_steps: Maya to send draft POC SOW and pricing by 2026-11-02
Liam to share benchmark template and sample scripts by 2026-11-03
Phoenix to export 7 days of token-level traffic and sample prompts by 2026-11-06
Schedule on-prem connectivity dry run for week of 2026-11-09
action_items: Maya Chen - Send POC SOW and cost estimate - due 2026-11-02
Liam O'Connor - Provide benchmark harness (k6 + sample loader) and runbook - due 2026-11-03
Tom Reynolds - Export token/tps distribution for last 7 days and SLO targets - due 2026-11-06
Aisha Patel - Provide top 20 prompt families and golden responses for quality checks - due 2026-11-06
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-29 16:00 PT
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Phoenix Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Infra), Nikhil Verma (CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — audio ok?
[00:05] Aisha Patel: Yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:07] Liam O'Connor: Good. I'll share a quick diagram in the chat of the reserved plus burst topology.
[00:12] Nikhil Verma: Cool. Our objective today is to nail down the POC success criteria and the capacity plan, especially for Black Friday-like spikes — though for Phoenix it's more of a regional sale pattern.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great. We'll cover proposed baseline reserved GPUs, burst pool sizing, and fallback rules. Also want to align on what you'll measure so we can pass/fail the pilot.
[00:30] Tom Reynolds: For context, our traffic today for the recommendation/chat endpoint averages 55 rps during peak, but we see short bursts up to 400 rps for 30–90s during promo pushes. Token sizes average ~220 tokens per request, sometimes up to 1k for long context.
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: That helps. So baseline 55 rps steady, spike to 400 rps short-duration. Two knobs we typically use: reserved capacity (dedicated GPUs) to handle steady, and a burst pool that can scale out with best-effort throughput. Fallbacks are critical — we can route to smaller quantized model or return graceful degraded response.
[01:05] Aisha Patel: Degraded response to what extent? We can't return nonsense. We need a quality gate — if the quantized model drops quality on our key prompts beyond x% we want automatic fallback to a cached prefix or a shorter answer.
[01:18] Liam O'Connor: Totally. We usually instrument a golden prompt set and track similarity metrics (BLEU / embedding cosine). For the POC we propose a 5% allowable drop in embedding similarity on the 20 golden prompts. If the drop exceeds that, the policy routes to cache-first or an alternate model variant.
[01:34] Nikhil Verma: That 5% figure — is that something Redwood recommends or typical from your other retailers?
[01:39] Maya Chen: It's a starting point. We've seen customers accept 3–8% depending on feature. For recommendations it's tighter; for chat exploratory it's looser. We can make it configurable per-route.
[01:48] Tom Reynolds: On infra — our security team requires that all PII is not persisted outside our VPC. For a private POC, do you support on-prem or VPC-private deployments?
[01:58] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We have a Private deployment option — customer-managed VPC peering + a lightweight control plane. For this POC we recommend Redwood Private in your AWS account with KMS integration so keys never leave your environment. There's some setup time — ~5 business days for connectivity and IAM roles.
[02:16] Aisha Patel: Ok timeline note.
[02:18] Maya Chen: On sizing: based on 55 rps steady with 220 tokens average, and a target 95th latency < 350ms, our initial reserved profile would be 2x A100-equivalent GPUs (or equivalent T4s if you choose a cheaper perf tradeoff) — that gives headroom for steady load plus smaller batching. For burst to 400 rps short windows, you'd add a burst pool of 6-8 gpus that spin up quickly, with autoscale floor/ceiling.
[02:43] Tom Reynolds: Can you quantify cost delta between reserved 2 GPUs vs reserved 4 GPUs to avoid bursting too often? We want to compare committed vs burst cost.
[02:51] Maya Chen: We'll run numbers in the SOW. Very rough: reserved 2 GPUs month-to-month vs reserved 4 could cut burst charges but increases base commit. For a 6-week POC, committed cost difference is material; we'll show a model.
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: Also quantization options can reduce GPU memory and increase throughput. We can recommend a 4-bit quantized variant for burst traffic — quicker to spin up and cheaper per-token — but quality needs to be validated against your golden prompts.
[03:21] Aisha Patel: About benchmarks — what do you need from us to run realistic tests?
[03:25] Liam O'Connor: Two things: (1) traffic distribution (tps by minute, token-size histogram) for the last 7 days, and (2) representative prompt families and golden responses. We'll provide a k6-based harness and a script that replays traffic at scale.
[03:39] Tom Reynolds: We'll export logs — be aware some of it has masked PII. We can provide synthetic but statistically similar token/tps profile.
[03:46] Maya Chen: That's fine. For the POC pass criteria, let's list what we expect:
[03:51] Liam O'Connor: 1) 95th percentile latency < 350ms for production model under baseline load, 2) burst availability with fallback < 99% successful request rate during spike windows, 3) quality regression < 5% on golden prompts for quantized/fallback variants, 4) operational metrics and dashboards in Redwood Console visible to Phoenix.
[04:10] Aisha Patel: Also need audit logs for all inference requests for compliance.
[04:14] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we can ship request-level audit logs to your S3 with encryption and signing.
[04:19] Nikhil Verma: How about cold start time for burst GPUs? If a spike hits and it takes 90s to spin up, that's bad.
[04:26] Liam O'Connor: Good point. We recommend a warm pool strategy: maintain a small warm buffer of 1–2 pre-warmed nodes that can immediately accept connections, plus rapid scale to target within ~20–45s depending on gfx. For even faster response we serve from the quantized variant during ramp and then shift traffic to the full model when ready.
[04:45] Tom Reynolds: So fallback routes would be: primary model on reserved GPUs -> quantized model on burst -> cache/short answer if both overloaded?
[04:53] Maya Chen: Exactly. And we can implement traffic shaping so you can prioritize certain users or routes.
[04:58] Aisha Patel: On benchmarks, we want both latency and quality measurements. Can you produce a combined report that shows tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, latency percentiles, and quality deltas?
[05:10] Liam O'Connor: Yes, that's the standard POC report we provide. We'll include cost modeling for 6-week extrapolation.
[05:16] Maya Chen: Timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) align on SOW and data; week 1-2 infra setup and connectivity; week 3 run baseline benchmarks; week 4 run spike/burst tests; week 5 analyze results and iterate; week 6 sign-off or remediation. That fits in a 6-week window.
[05:33] Nikhil Verma: Sounds good, but infra team needs two full weeks for approvals. That pushes the run by two weeks — still ok, we can aim for a 8-week calendar but keep POC duration as 6 active weeks.
[05:44] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include that contingency in the SOW.
[05:47] Aisha Patel: Security: we need SOC2 attestation and support for customer-managed KMS; we also need data retention policies — logs to be deleted after 90 days unless requested.
[05:58] Liam O'Connor: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and supports KMS integrations; retention windows are configurable and we'll include that in the security addendum.
[06:06] Tom Reynolds: Any major blockers you see?
[06:08] Maya Chen: Nothing major. The only potential risk is if your spike pattern is much higher than described or token sizes are often >1k, which would change GPU counts. We'll validate once you send the traffic histograms.
[06:19] Aisha Patel: Recap and next steps?
[06:21] Maya Chen: Recap: I'll send draft SOW and rough cost model by 11/02; Liam will send benchmark harness and runbook by 11/03; Tom/Aisha to share traffic dumps and prompt set by 11/06; schedule connectivity dry run for week of 11/09 — any objections?
[06:36] Nikhil Verma: No objections.
[06:38] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good.
[06:40] Aisha Patel: Great, thanks everyone.
[06:42] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links to the harness and the SOW. Bye.

End of transcript.
